options.text: Normal polling traffic that needs no action
Write requests the historian should never send
Diagnostic counters being read by the historian
Device identification queries by an inventory tool

explanation: Modbus function code 16 is Write Multiple Registers, so a read-only historian sending it suggests compromise or misconfiguration and warrants investigation. Normal historian polling would use read function codes such as 03. Diagnostics use function code 08. Device identification uses the encapsulated interface function code 43.

prompt: Packet capture on a utility's SCADA network shows a DNP3 message with function code 13 (cold restart) sent to an outstation from a host that is not the SCADA master. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: The SCADA master is performing a routine integrity poll
The outstation is confirming receipt of a read request
An unauthorized restart command to the outstation
The outstation is reporting an unsolicited event

explanation: DNP3 function code 13 is a cold restart command, and receiving it from a host other than the master suggests unauthorized control activity that could take the outstation offline. Unsolicited event reports are responses from outstations, not restart requests. An integrity poll is a read request from the master. Confirmations do not use the cold restart function code.

prompt: A PLC's audit log shows a program download at 02:14 from the engineering workstation. No change request or maintenance was scheduled. Which TWO data sources should the analyst examine next to determine who performed the download? (Choose two.)

options.text: The plant's visitor parking records
Remote access and jump host session logs for that time
The historian's trend of ambient temperature
Logon and identity logs on the engineering workstation
Weather data for the night of the change

explanation: Identity and logon logs on the workstation and session logs from the remote access path or jump host show which account and session were active at 02:14. Ambient temperature trends, parking records and weather data cannot attribute the program download to a user or session.

prompt: Operators report that a tank's high-level alarm limit seems to change by itself. The historian shows the limit changing several times overnight. What should the analyst correlate with these process log entries?

options.text: HMI and controller change logs and sessions at those times
The control building's lighting and HVAC schedule
Corporate email gateway spam statistics for that same night
Printer usage logs from the administration building

explanation: Correlating process log changes with HMI and controller change logs and user sessions at the same times shows whether a person, an account or a program made the changes. Spam statistics, lighting schedules and printer logs have no connection to alarm limit changes in the control system.

prompt: Firewall logs at the boundary of a PLC zone show hundreds of denied connection attempts from the IDMZ jump host to sequential IP addresses in the PLC subnet on TCP 502 and TCP 44818. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A failing firewall power supply
The PLCs sending unsolicited responses to the IDMZ
Normal historian replication from the IDMZ
Scanning from a possibly compromised jump host

explanation: Sequential connection attempts across addresses on industrial ports indicate scanning, and a jump host performing it suggests compromise or misuse. Historian replication would use a few defined flows to known hosts. A failing power supply would not generate structured denied-connection logs. The connections originate from the jump host, not from the PLCs.

prompt: A managed switch in a control panel logs a link-up event and a new MAC address with a consumer laptop manufacturer's prefix on a normally unused port at 23:40. No work was scheduled. What should the analyst conclude?

options.text: A PLC has changed its MAC address after a power cycle
An unauthorized device may have been connected
Spanning tree is reconverging normally after a link change
The switch is performing a scheduled firmware update

explanation: A new, unexpected MAC address from a laptop manufacturer on an unused port outside a work window suggests an unauthorized device. Firmware updates do not create link-up events with new MAC addresses. PLC MAC addresses are fixed in hardware and would not show a laptop maker's prefix. Spanning tree reconvergence does not introduce a new end device.

prompt: An analyst trying to reconstruct an attack finds that firewall, switch and server logs disagree by several minutes about when events happened, making correlation unreliable. Which fix should be made first?

options.text: Increase log retention on every device to two years
Convert all collected logs to PDF files for review
Disable logging on the switches to reduce the noise
Synchronize all devices to a common trusted NTP source

explanation: Accurate correlation across syslog sources depends on synchronized clocks, so devices should use a common trusted time source. Longer retention does not fix inconsistent timestamps. Disabling switch logging removes a data source. Converting logs to PDF makes them harder to search and does not correct times.

prompt: TACACS+ accounting records show that an administrator account ran commands on an OT firewall at 03:00 that added an allow rule from the corporate network to the PLC zone. No change was approved. What data has revealed this?

options.text: AAA accounting logs from the network device
Endpoint protection quarantine logs from the HMIs
Network performance monitoring latency graphs
Historian trend data for the PLC zone

explanation: AAA accounting logs, such as TACACS+ accounting, record which account ran which commands on network devices and when. EPP quarantine logs record malware actions on hosts. NPM graphs show performance metrics, not commands. Historian trends show process values, not administrative commands.

prompt: Windows security logs on an HMI show about 300 failed logons (event ID 4625) for the operator account within ten minutes, followed by a successful logon (event ID 4624) for the same account from an unfamiliar IP address. What is the most likely conclusion?

options.text: An operator mistyped a password once
Windows Update installed a patch
A password-guessing attack has probably succeeded
The HMI clock drifted and generated duplicate events

explanation: Hundreds of failures followed by a success from an unfamiliar source is the pattern of a successful brute-force or password-guessing attack. A single mistyped password would not produce hundreds of failures. Windows Update activity does not generate logon failures. Clock drift changes timestamps but does not create new logon events.

prompt: An EDR product on HMIs is configured to kill processes and isolate the host automatically on high-severity detections. After a false positive stopped an HMI runtime during production, the plant must retune the EDR policy. What is the best approach?

options.text: Alert only, with vendor exclusions and human-approved isolation
Keep automatic isolation and lower the HMI alert threshold further
Uninstall the EDR agent from all HMIs permanently
Exclude the entire system drive from EDR monitoring

explanation: For OT hosts, EDR policies are usually tuned to detect and alert, with vendor-validated exclusions, while disruptive responses such as isolation require human approval. Removing EDR discards detection. Keeping automatic isolation with a lower threshold makes disruptions more likely. Excluding the whole system drive blinds the EDR.

prompt: During a hypothesis-driven threat hunt on engineering workstations, which artifact would most strongly suggest that an attacker created a persistence mechanism?

options.text: A DHCP lease renewal for the workstation
A routine Windows Update installation record
An HMI alarm acknowledgement entry by an operator
System event 7045: new service from a temp folder

explanation: Windows System event 7045 records a newly installed service, and a service binary in a temporary directory is a common persistence artifact. A routine update record is expected activity. Alarm acknowledgements are normal operator actions. DHCP lease renewals are routine network activity.

prompt: An OT IDS rule that alerts on PLC program downloads generates dozens of alerts during every planned maintenance outage, and analysts have started ignoring it. What is the best tuning action?

options.text: Delete all alerts generated during outages without review
Change the rule so that it never generates high-severity alerts again
Suppress approved hosts in change windows and alert on the rest
Disable the program download rule permanently

explanation: Tuning should keep the detection's value by suppressing known-good activity, such as downloads from authorized hosts during approved windows, while alerting on everything else. Disabling the rule removes detection of unauthorized downloads. Downgrading severity hides real events. Deleting alerts without review loses evidence and discards the detection.

prompt: A review of rule hit counts on an OT boundary firewall shows several allow rules that have had zero hits in 18 months and were created for a system that has been decommissioned. What should be done?

options.text: Move them to the top of the rule base for faster matching
Confirm with owners, then remove them via change management
Leave them in place in case the old system is ever returned
Convert them to allow any service between the same hosts

explanation: Unused rules for decommissioned systems widen the attack surface and should be removed after owner confirmation under change control. Keeping them in case the system returns leaves unnecessary openings. Moving them to the top changes evaluation order without reducing exposure. Allowing any service makes them more permissive.

prompt: A network performance monitoring tool shows that latency on a control network ring jumped and broadcast traffic increased sharply at the same time several HMIs lost communication. What should the analyst consider?

options.text: A broadcast storm, loop or scan consuming bandwidth
The SIEM license for the plant has expired
The historian's data disk has filled up completely
The HMIs need updated screen graphics and faceplates

explanation: A sudden rise in broadcast traffic and latency matching communication losses suggests a broadcast storm, a network loop or scanning, which NPM data helps trace. HMI graphics do not affect network latency. A full historian disk would affect data storage, not network-wide latency. An expired SIEM license would not change network traffic.

prompt: A plant is configuring SOAR playbooks for alerts from its OT monitoring platform. Which automated action is most appropriate without human approval?

options.text: Automatically rebooting HMIs that show suspicious processes
Enriching alerts with context and opening a ticket
Automatically blocking all traffic to a PLC that triggered an alert
Automatically disabling the operator accounts involved in any alert

explanation: Enrichment and ticket creation are safe automations that speed analysis without affecting the process. Automatically blocking PLC traffic, rebooting HMIs or disabling operator accounts could disrupt operations or safety, so in OT such actions should require human approval.

prompt: A vendor has released a patch for a vulnerability in an HMI application, but the patch requires a newer HMI version, which in turn requires a newer operating system than the plant runs. Which patch consideration is this?

options.text: Availability
Viability
Applicability
Dependency

explanation: A dependency exists when applying the patch requires other changes first, here an HMI upgrade and a new OS. Applicability asks whether the vulnerability affects the installed product at all. Availability asks whether a patch exists and when the system can be taken offline. Viability asks whether applying it is practical and supported in this environment.

prompt: A Windows security update is available, but the DCS vendor has not yet qualified it for the installed DCS release and warns that unqualified patches may void support. Which patch consideration is the main concern?

options.text: Spare availability
Dependency
Viability
Applicability

explanation: Viability concerns whether a patch can be practically applied in this environment, including whether the vendor supports it with the installed system. Applicability concerns whether the vulnerability affects the system. Dependency concerns prerequisite changes. Spare availability concerns having replacement hardware on hand.

prompt: A compliance standard requires MFA for interactive access to control system hosts, but a legacy HMI cannot support MFA. The plant instead restricts the HMI to a badge-controlled control room and requires MFA on the jump host that is the only remote path to it. What are these alternative measures?

options.text: Compensating controls
Risk transfer
Rollback plan
Version management

explanation: Compensating controls are alternative measures used in place of a required control that cannot be implemented, providing comparable protection. Risk transfer shifts consequences to another party. Version management tracks software and firmware versions. A rollback plan describes how to reverse a change.

prompt: A critical vulnerability in a PLC's web server cannot be patched until the next turnaround in eight months. In the meantime, the team disables the web server and blocks HTTP to the PLC at the zone firewall. What type of remediation is this?

options.text: Risk acceptance
Mitigating controls
Bare metal recovery
Version management

explanation: Mitigating controls reduce the likelihood or impact of exploiting a vulnerability while a permanent fix is pending, such as disabling the service and blocking the port. Version management tracks and standardizes versions. Risk acceptance would leave the vulnerability without new controls. Bare metal recovery is a restoration method.

prompt: A plant has 60 identical drives running five different firmware versions because updates were applied inconsistently. Which practice would most help vulnerability remediation?

options.text: Allowing technicians to choose any firmware they prefer
Removing firmware versions from the asset inventory
Version management standardizing on approved releases
Replacing all drives with a different brand

explanation: Version management records which versions are installed and keeps devices on approved releases, making it easier to identify exposure and plan updates. Removing versions from the inventory hides exposure. Letting technicians choose firmware increases inconsistency. Replacing every drive is costly and does not by itself create version control.

prompt: Two vulnerabilities are found: one is listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and affects internet-reachable remote access appliances; the other has no known exploitation and affects isolated Level 1 controllers. How should the remediation timeline differ?

options.text: The isolated controller should be fixed first because it is more critical
Neither needs a timeline because both are low risk
Both must be remediated on the same day
The actively exploited, exposed appliance should get a much shorter timeline

explanation: Remediation timelines should reflect risk, and active exploitation combined with internet exposure calls for urgent action. Treating both identically ignores the differences in likelihood. Criticality matters, but an isolated controller with no known exploitation is less urgent than an exposed, exploited device. Neither is low risk, and both need a timeline.

prompt: A firmware fix for compressor controllers requires stopping the compressors, which run continuously. The next scheduled plant shutdown is in four months, and the vulnerability is mitigated by firewall rules. Which approach to the remediation implementation window is most appropriate?

options.text: Never apply the update because the compressors cannot stop
Use the planned shutdown and keep mitigations until then
Apply the update remotely while the compressors are running
Stop the compressors immediately without telling operations

explanation: With mitigations in place, aligning the update with planned downtime minimizes operational impact while still remediating. Stopping the compressors without coordination disrupts operations and may create safety issues. Never applying the fix leaves the vulnerability indefinitely. Updating firmware on running controllers that require a stop risks an unplanned trip.

prompt: Before updating the firmware of a unique protective relay for which the plant has no spare, the engineer learns that a failed update could leave the relay inoperable. Which coordination step reduces this risk most directly?

options.text: Perform the update without a backup to save time
Ask the ISAC to approve the update
Disable protection on the circuit during the update without notifying anyone
Ensure a spare relay is available, or procure one, before performing the update

explanation: Having a spare on hand means a failed update can be recovered quickly by swapping hardware, which is a key remediation consideration for unique devices. Skipping backups increases risk. Disabling protection without coordination is a serious safety hazard. ISACs share information and do not approve changes.

prompt: Just before a scheduled HMI patching window, the technician discovers that the last successful backup of the HMI server is eight months old. What should happen?

options.text: Take and verify a current backup first, or reschedule
Proceed, because vendor patches rarely fail in practice
Patch first and then take a backup afterward
Cancel the patching permanently for this server

explanation: Backup availability is a precondition for remediation, so a current, verified backup should be taken before patching, or the work rescheduled. Proceeding without one risks unrecoverable failure. Cancelling permanently leaves the vulnerability. Backing up afterward captures the patched state and does not help if the patch fails.

prompt: Before rolling out a controller firmware update across a plant, the team installs it on an identical controller in a test bed running a copy of the production logic and observes I/O, communications and scan time. Which remediation step is this?

options.text: Risk transfer
Implementation
Testing
Process validation

explanation: Testing on a representative test bed before production checks compatibility and performance. Implementation is deploying the update to production. Process validation confirms the production process runs correctly after implementation. Risk transfer shifts consequences to another party.

prompt: After a firmware update is installed on a production PLC, the device boots normally and its diagnostics are green. What should the team do before closing the change?

options.text: Delete the backup of the previous firmware to avoid confusion
Close the change because the PLC booted and diagnostics are green
Immediately apply the next available firmware update as well
Validate the process with operations, including I/O and interlocks

explanation: Process validation confirms that the controlled process works correctly after a change, including I/O, interlocks and loop behavior, not just that the device boots. A successful boot does not prove correct control. Deleting the previous backup removes the rollback option. Applying another update immediately adds untested change.

prompt: A vendor's release notes state that once a new firmware version is installed on its safety controller, the device cannot be downgraded. How should this affect remediation planning?

options.text: Prepare another rollback path, such as a spare with old firmware
The team should install the update on all controllers at once
The team should remove the controller from the asset inventory
None, because a firmware rollback is never actually needed

explanation: Rollback plan availability must be confirmed before remediation, and if downgrade is impossible an alternative such as a spare with the previous firmware must be prepared. Rollback can always be needed if an update causes problems. Updating all controllers at once increases risk when rollback is limited. Removing the controller from the inventory hides the asset.

prompt: An OT security team subscribes to CISA ICS advisories, vendor PSIRT notices and ISAC bulletins, and checks each new item against its installed base. What type of vulnerability identification is this?

options.text: Internal vulnerability identification
Bare metal analysis
External vulnerability identification
Penetration testing

explanation: Learning of vulnerabilities from outside sources such as government advisories, vendors and ISACs is external vulnerability identification. Internal identification uses the organization's own assessments, scans and reviews. Penetration testing actively exploits weaknesses. Bare metal analysis is not a vulnerability identification method.

prompt: During an in-house configuration review, plant engineers find that several switches still use default SNMP community strings and that one HMI has file sharing open to everyone. No advisory mentions these issues. What type of identification is this?

options.text: Risk transfer
Internal vulnerability identification
Threat intelligence dissemination
External vulnerability identification

explanation: Weaknesses found through the organization's own reviews, scans or assessments are internal vulnerability identification, which often finds configuration issues no advisory will mention. External identification relies on outside sources. Threat intelligence dissemination is a stage of the intelligence cycle. Risk transfer is a risk treatment.

prompt: A plant's OT monitoring platform reads firmware versions from normal traffic captured at a SPAN port and matches them to published CVEs, without sending any packets to the controllers. Which detection method is this?

options.text: Passive
Credentialed
Active
Destructive

explanation: Passive detection infers vulnerabilities from observed traffic without interacting with devices, which is safe for fragile controllers. Active detection sends probes or queries. Credentialed scanning logs in to hosts to inspect them, which is a form of active scanning. Destructive testing is not a standard detection method and would be unsafe.

prompt: The team wants detailed patch levels for its Windows HMI and historian servers, including missing updates and insecure settings. The vendor approves an authenticated scan during a maintenance window. Which detection method is this?

options.text: Passive
Active
Manual walkdown
Derived

explanation: Authenticated scanning interacts directly with the hosts and is an active method, giving detailed results but requiring vendor approval and careful scheduling. Passive methods only observe traffic. Derived methods infer vulnerabilities from existing data such as inventory records. A manual walkdown is physical inspection.

prompt: Without scanning or capturing traffic, an analyst compares model and firmware fields in the CMDB with a newly published advisory and identifies 14 affected controllers. Which detection method is this?

options.text: Fuzzing
Active
Derived
Passive

explanation: Derived detection infers vulnerabilities from data already held, such as inventory or CMDB attributes matched to advisories. Active detection probes devices. Passive detection observes live traffic. Fuzzing sends malformed input to find new flaws and is unsafe on production OT.

prompt: A widely used open-source logging library is found to have a critical vulnerability. The plant needs to know which of its OT software products embed that library, even though it is not listed as a separate installed application. Which data source helps most?

options.text: Network performance monitoring data
Badge access logs for the control room
The plant's lockout/tagout permit records
Vendor-supplied software bills of materials

explanation: A software bill of materials lists the components inside a software product, revealing embedded libraries that do not appear as separate applications. NPM data shows network performance. Badge logs show physical access. Lockout/tagout records document energy isolation.

prompt: An analyst wants standardized information for a CVE, including its CVSS base score, affected product identifiers (CPE) and references, to enrich a vulnerability ticket. Which public source provides this?

options.text: The MITRE ATT&CK for ICS matrix
An IDMZ firewall log
A YARA rule repository
The National Vulnerability Database

explanation: The NVD, maintained by NIST, enriches CVE records with CVSS scores, CPE product identifiers and references. YARA repositories hold malware detection rules. ATT&CK for ICS describes adversary techniques, not individual CVEs. Firewall logs record traffic, not vulnerability details.

prompt: A CVE entry in a public database lists a PLC product family as affected but gives no mitigations specific to the plant's module. The analyst needs exact affected firmware ranges, fixed versions and workarounds for that module. Where should the analyst look?

options.text: A general security news site's summary
The plant's own change management log
The vendor's security advisory for the product
A social media post discussing the CVE

explanation: The vendor advisory is usually the authoritative source for exact affected versions, fixes and product-specific workarounds. News sites summarize but may be incomplete. Social media posts are unverified. The change log records changes already made at the plant, not vulnerability details.

prompt: An advisory describes a vulnerability in a PLC communications module that can be exploited only when the module's embedded web server is enabled. The plant disabled the web server on all modules during hardening, and inventory confirms this. How should the finding be triaged?

options.text: Highest priority, because the CVSS base score is high
Low relevance; document and monitor the setting
Remove the affected modules from the asset inventory
Enable the web server to confirm the vulnerability exists

explanation: Triage considers applicability and relevance: if the vulnerable feature is disabled and verified, the risk is much lower, though the configuration should be documented and monitored. A high CVSS score alone does not account for the environment. Enabling the web server would create the exposure. Removing modules from inventory hides assets.

prompt: Two vulnerabilities need prioritizing. The first has a CVSS score of 9.8 but affects a controller in an isolated test lab with no network path to production. The second has a score of 7.5, has a public exploit, is actively exploited and affects an internet-facing remote access gateway into the plant. Which should be remediated first, and why?

options.text: The second, because it is exposed and actively exploited
Neither, because CVSS scores below 10 are not urgent
The first, because a higher CVSS score always means higher priority
Both at the same time, because prioritization is not appropriate in OT

explanation: Prioritization weighs exposure, exploitability, relevance, severity and impact, so an exposed, actively exploited gateway outranks an isolated lab device with a higher base score. CVSS severity alone does not reflect environment or threat activity. Vulnerabilities below a perfect score can still be urgent. Prioritization is essential in OT because resources and downtime are limited.

prompt: Engineers report that a firmware update fixing a critical vulnerability has been applied to 40 controllers. How should the security team verify the remediation?

options.text: Independently confirm every device reports the fixed version
Wait for the next external audit to check
Accept the engineers' report and close the ticket
Assume success because the update was applied during an outage

explanation: Remediation verification confirms independently that each affected device now runs the fixed version, using passive monitoring, vendor tools or updated inventory. Accepting a report without checking can miss devices that failed to update. Applying an update during an outage does not guarantee success. Waiting for an audit leaves unverified risk for months.

prompt: A plant requires every USB drive entering the facility to be checked before it can be used on any OT system. Which control best supports this?

options.text: Asking each visitor to confirm that the drive is clean
A scanning kiosk with anti-malware engines at the entrance
Allowing drives only on scheduled maintenance days
Plugging the drive into an HMI to check its contents

explanation: A scanning kiosk with anti-malware engines inspects removable media before it reaches OT systems. Asking visitors relies on trust and provides no inspection. Plugging an unscanned drive into an HMI exposes the very system the control protects. Restricting the day of use provides no inspection.

prompt: A plant issues a set of USB drives that may be used only on OT systems for transferring PLC programs and must never be connected to corporate or personal computers. What is this control called?

options.text: Data loss detection
Write blocking
Geolocation
Dedicated devices

explanation: Dedicated devices are reserved for a single purpose or environment, reducing the chance of picking up malware from other networks. Data loss detection identifies unauthorized data transfers. A write blocker prevents writes to media during forensic acquisition. Geolocation determines device location.

prompt: The OT security team configures HMIs to accept only USB storage devices whose serial numbers appear on an approved list, blocking all others automatically. Which removable media control is this?

options.text: Destruction
Procurement
Authorization
Sanitization

explanation: Authorization limits use to approved media, here enforced through device control based on serial numbers. Destruction physically renders media unusable at the end of its life. Sanitization removes data from media for reuse or disposal. Procurement concerns how media are purchased.

prompt: A failed solid-state drive from an engineering workstation held PLC projects and network diagrams. It cannot be powered up to wipe it, and it will not be reused. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Throw it in the general waste bin after removing labels
Reformat it on another computer before disposal
Physically destroy it and record the destruction
Store it indefinitely in an unlocked drawer

explanation: Media containing sensitive data that cannot be sanitized and will not be reused should be physically destroyed, consistent with NIST SP 800-88's destroy method, and documented. General waste disposal exposes the data. A failed drive cannot be reformatted, and reformatting does not reliably remove data from SSDs. An unlocked drawer leaves the data accessible.

prompt: A plant wants to reuse USB drives that previously carried files from a contractor's laptop. Which step is required before the drives are reissued for OT use?

options.text: Sanitize them with an approved method
Label them with the previous user's name
Store them for a week before reuse
Rename all the files stored on them

explanation: Sanitization removes prior data and hidden content using an approved method, such as those in NIST SP 800-88, before media are reused. Renaming files leaves the contents intact. Storing drives for a week changes nothing about their contents. Labeling them does not remove data or malware.

prompt: Engineers have collected free USB drives at a trade show and want to use them to move files between OT systems. What does the removable media procurement policy most likely require instead?

options.text: Asking colleagues for spare drives from home
Buying approved media from trusted suppliers
Using the free drives after a quick visual inspection
Using any drive as long as it has a manufacturer logo

explanation: Procurement controls require media to come from trusted suppliers through approved channels, since giveaway or unknown drives can carry malware or tampered firmware. A visual inspection cannot detect malicious firmware or files. A logo does not prove provenance. Drives from home have unknown history.

prompt: An auditor asks the plant to show which approved USB drives exist, who has each one and when each was last returned. Which control provides this?

options.text: Drive encryption
Network access control on switches
Write blocking on each issued drive
Tracking with a check-out and check-in log

explanation: Tracking media through a check-out and check-in log by serial number shows inventory, custody and return history. Write blocking prevents changes during forensic acquisition. Encryption protects data on media but does not record custody. Network access control governs network connections, not USB custody.

prompt: A USB drive found plugged into an HMI is suspected of carrying malware. The incident responder wants to image it for analysis without changing any data on it. What should be used?

options.text: The HMI itself, so the image matches the original context
A drive formatter
A hardware write blocker on a forensic workstation
A scanning kiosk that deletes infected files

explanation: A hardware write blocker allows read-only acquisition, preserving the evidence for analysis. Using the HMI risks executing malware and changing the media. A kiosk that deletes infected files alters the evidence. Formatting destroys the evidence.

prompt: Engineering laptops used as transient devices are stored between jobs in a locked cabinet. Each laptop case is closed with a serialized tamper-evident seal. What should a technician do when checking out a laptop?

options.text: Verify the seal is intact and matches the log
Ignore the seal if the laptop powers on normally
Break the seal and record nothing in the log
Replace the seal with ordinary tape after use

explanation: Tamper-proofing validation means checking that seals are intact and match recorded serial numbers, revealing possible interference during storage. Breaking the seal without recording it defeats the control. Tape does not provide tamper evidence. A laptop that powers on normally may still have been tampered with.

prompt: An integrator arrives with a company laptop and needs to connect to a control network to commission a new skid. Which approach best manages the risk from this third-party laptop?

options.text: Allow it to connect immediately because the integrator is under contract
Posture-check it before a controlled connection, or lend a plant laptop
Connect it only to the corporate guest Wi-Fi first to download updates
Ask the integrator to sign a form stating that the laptop is clean

explanation: Third-party laptops should pass a posture check before a controlled connection, or the plant can supply its own managed laptop. A contract does not ensure the laptop is clean. Connecting to guest Wi-Fi first exposes it to more networks without verifying it. A signed form is an assurance, not a technical check.

prompt: Instrument technicians use handheld calibrators and HART communicators that connect directly to field transmitters and can change their configuration. How should these devices be treated in the security program?

options.text: As out of scope, because they are not general-purpose computers
As permanent network infrastructure
As personal property of the technicians
As transient devices that are inventoried and controlled

explanation: Calibration equipment that connects to and can reconfigure field devices is a transient device that should be inventoried, controlled and checked. Being non-PC hardware does not remove the risk. These devices are not permanent infrastructure. Tools used on plant equipment should be company-controlled, not personal property.

prompt: A plant is updating its policy on phones, tablets and wearables such as smartwatches in the control room. Which TWO measures are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Encourage staff to photograph HMI screens to share on social media
Let tablets join the control network using the shared operator password
Allow personal smartwatches to pair with HMIs over Bluetooth for notifications
Restrict cameras and wireless features of personal devices in sensitive areas where screens and drawings are visible
Prohibit personal devices from connecting to OT networks or charging from OT equipment

explanation: Keeping personal devices off OT networks and charging ports, and restricting cameras and wireless features in sensitive areas, reduce malware and information leakage risks. Pairing smartwatches with HMIs adds an unmanaged wireless path. Photographing HMI screens for social media discloses sensitive information. Joining tablets with a shared password undermines authentication.

prompt: A vendor's skid includes a cellular modem that stays connected at all times so the vendor can monitor performance. How should the plant treat this connection?

options.text: As a temporary external connection that needs no inventory record
As acceptable as long as it is not mentioned in the contract
As a persistent external connection to inventory and secure
As irrelevant because it does not use the plant's internet circuit

explanation: An always-on cellular modem is a persistent external connection that bypasses plant boundaries, so it must be inventoried, assessed and secured or removed. It is not temporary. Using a separate carrier makes it a hidden path, not an irrelevant one. Leaving it out of the contract removes accountability rather than reducing risk.

prompt: A plant's vendor works only from one country, but the remote access gateway logs show login attempts with the vendor's credentials from several other countries. Which control would help block these attempts while allowing legitimate access?

options.text: Sharing the vendor account with more users
Increasing the gateway session timeout
Disabling remote access logs
Geolocation-based access restrictions

explanation: Geolocation restrictions limit connections to expected regions, blocking credential use from unexpected countries, ideally alongside MFA. A longer session timeout increases exposure. Disabling logs removes visibility. Sharing the account weakens accountability and increases risk.

prompt: An endpoint agent on an engineering workstation alerts that an entire folder of PLC project files and network drawings was copied to an unapproved USB drive minutes before a contractor's last day. Which control generated this alert?

options.text: Data loss detection
Write blocker
Turnstile access logging
Secure Boot

explanation: Data loss detection monitors for sensitive data leaving through channels such as removable media and alerts on unauthorized transfers. A write blocker prevents writing to media during forensic work. Secure Boot verifies boot components. Turnstile logs record physical entries, not file copies.

prompt: Before any incident occurs, an OT security team writes its response plan, trains staff, gathers contact lists, pre-stages forensic tools and confirms that backups can be restored. Which PICERL phase is this?

options.text: Identify
Prepare
Lessons learned
Recover

explanation: The Prepare phase covers everything done in advance so the organization can respond effectively, including plans, training, tools and verified backups. Identify detects and confirms incidents. Recover restores operations after eradication. Lessons learned reviews the response after the incident.

prompt: Operators report odd HMI behavior. The response team reviews alerts and logs, confirms that an unauthorized account changed set points, and determines which systems are affected. Which PICERL phase does this activity represent?

options.text: Eradicate
Contain
Prepare
Identify

explanation: The Identify phase determines whether an event is an incident and establishes its nature and scope. Contain limits the spread and impact once the incident is confirmed. Eradicate removes the cause. Prepare happens before any incident.

prompt: Responders have isolated an infected HMI zone from the rest of the plant network, and the process is being run safely from local panels. According to the PICERL model, which phase comes next?

options.text: Identify
Prepare
Eradicate
Lessons learned

explanation: PICERL proceeds Prepare, Identify, Contain, Eradicate, Recover and Lessons learned, so after containment the team removes the malware and the attacker's access. Prepare happens before incidents. Lessons learned comes after recovery. Identification has already confirmed the incident.

prompt: After malware has been removed, the team rebuilds HMIs from known-good images, restores PLC programs from verified backups and works with operations to return the process to normal production. Which PICERL phase is this?

options.text: Identify
Recover
Contain
Lessons learned

explanation: Recover restores systems and operations to normal after eradication, including rebuilding hosts and validating the process. Contain limits the incident's spread. Identify confirms and scopes it. Lessons learned reviews the response once recovery is complete.

prompt: Two weeks after an incident, operations, engineering, IT and security meet to review what happened, what worked, what did not and which plans and controls must change. Which PICERL phase is this?

options.text: Lessons learned
Contain
Eradicate
Prepare

explanation: The Lessons learned phase reviews the incident and response to improve plans, controls and training. Prepare involves building capability before incidents, although lessons learned feeds back into it. Eradicate removes the threat. Contain limits its spread.

prompt: A refinery wants its cyber incident response to use the same command structure that its emergency response teams use for fires and chemical releases, with an incident commander, defined sections and a common terminology, adapted for industrial cyber incidents. Which framework fits best?

options.text: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain model
The Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model (C2M2)
The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis
ICS4ICS (Incident Command System for ICS)

explanation: ICS4ICS adapts the Incident Command System, used by emergency responders, to cybersecurity incidents that affect industrial control systems, giving a common structure with an incident commander and defined roles. The Diamond Model analyzes intrusions. The Cyber Kill Chain describes attacker stages. C2M2 measures program maturity.

prompt: During a cyber incident, operators lose reliable control of a reactor's temperature and readings approach the safe operating limit. What should happen?

options.text: The SOC remotely reboots the DCS to clear the problem
The cybersecurity team decides whether to shut down after finishing its forensic collection
Operations initiates emergency shutdown per its procedures
The plant waits for approval from the insurer before acting

explanation: When safe limits are threatened, operations must initiate emergency shutdown according to established procedures; safety takes precedence over investigation. Forensics must never delay a safety action. An insurer has no role in immediate safety decisions. Remotely rebooting the DCS could remove control and worsen the situation.

prompt: A cyberattack on a chemical plant's control system causes a leak of a toxic gas into the surrounding area. What is the first physical response priority?

options.text: Notify the cyber insurer's breach hotline
Activate site emergency response and call emergency services
Draft a press release for local news outlets
Collect memory images from all HMIs before evacuating

explanation: A toxic release is a physical emergency, so the site emergency response must be activated and emergency services contacted to protect people. Memory collection is important but never ahead of life safety. A press release is part of crisis communication that comes later. Insurer notification is required but is not the first priority.

prompt: During a major OT ransomware incident, the CEO, legal counsel, communications and operations leaders meet to make business decisions, coordinate statements to the media and customers and approve major expenditures. What function are they performing?

options.text: Crisis management
Packet analysis
Vulnerability triage
Root cause analysis

explanation: Crisis management handles executive decision-making, communications, legal and business continuity during a major incident, while technical teams handle the response. Root cause analysis is a technical investigation. Vulnerability triage prioritizes weaknesses. Packet analysis examines network traffic.

prompt: During an OT incident, which statement best describes the roles of the facility's operations, engineering and maintenance groups?

options.text: Only maintenance should be involved, because it owns the tools
Operations runs the process; engineering advises; maintenance does field work
Engineering should take control of the process from operations
They should stay away from the response so that the security team can work alone

explanation: Each facility group contributes: operations keeps the process safe, engineering understands the logic and design, and maintenance carries out physical work. Excluding them removes essential knowledge and authority. Limiting involvement to maintenance ignores operations and engineering. Operations, not engineering, retains authority over running the process.

prompt: The corporate IT incident response playbook says to power off and reimage any host with suspected malware immediately. Malware is suspected on an HMI controlling a running continuous process. What is the best approach?

options.text: Follow the IT playbook and power off the HMI immediately to stop spread
Ignore the malware until the next planned shutdown of the unit
Coordinate with operations on alternate control before isolating the HMI
Reimage the PLCs as well as the HMI to be completely safe

explanation: OT response must account for process safety and availability, so actions on an HMI are coordinated with operations, who confirm alternative monitoring and control first. Powering off without coordination could leave operators blind. Ignoring the malware lets it spread. Reimaging PLCs is not justified by suspected HMI malware and could stop the process.

prompt: A small water utility suffers an incident affecting its SCADA system and lacks enough staff with OT forensic skills. Which TWO mutual aid options can it draw on? (Choose two.)

options.text: An incident response retainer with a firm that has OT experience
An anonymous online forum for posting raw logs
A volunteer with no vetting who offers help on social media
The PLC vendor's marketing department
Peer utilities and its sector ISAC

explanation: Peers and the sector ISAC can share expertise and information, and a pre-arranged incident response retainer provides vetted OT responders quickly. Posting raw logs on an anonymous forum exposes sensitive information. A marketing department cannot provide forensic help. An unvetted volunteer is a security risk.

prompt: An electric utility determines that an OT cyber incident meets its regulatory definition of a reportable incident. Which escalation and notification actions are required?

options.text: Notify no one until the investigation is completely finished
Post details of the incident on the company's social media
Notify only the equipment vendor's support desk
Escalate internally and report to required regulators and agencies on time

explanation: Escalation includes internal leadership, and reportable incidents must be reported to regulators and government agencies within the deadlines set by applicable rules. Waiting until the investigation ends can violate reporting deadlines. Social media is not a notification channel and may expose sensitive details. Notifying only the vendor does not meet regulatory obligations.

prompt: A manufacturer's plant is hit by an OT incident on a weekend when its own control engineers are unavailable. The company has a sister plant with engineers trained on the same DCS. Which type of mutual aid is the plant using when it borrows those engineers?

options.text: Internal mutual aid
Insurance-provided response
Peer mutual aid through an ISAC
An incident response retainer

explanation: Drawing on staff from elsewhere within the same organization is internal mutual aid. Peer mutual aid through an ISAC involves other organizations. An incident response retainer is a contract with an outside firm. Insurance-provided response comes from the insurer's approved vendors.

prompt: A manufacturer's incident response plan was written for corporate IT and does not mention control systems. What should be added when updating it into an OT incident response plan?

options.text: A requirement that only the IT help desk handles OT incidents
Instructions to wipe and reload all controllers after any security alert
Removal of all references to safety so the plan stays technical
OT roles, safety coordination, vendor contacts and shutdown criteria

explanation: An OT IRP must define OT roles, who can make process decisions, coordination with safety and operations, vendor contacts and when shutdown is required. Wiping controllers after any alert is dangerous and unnecessary. Limiting response to the IT help desk excludes the people who understand the process. Safety must be central to OT response, not removed.

prompt: A technician needs a document that lists the exact commands and steps to restore a specific HMI model from its golden image and reconnect it to the historian. Which document is this?

options.text: Business impact analysis
Policy
Runbook
Risk register

explanation: A runbook provides detailed, step-by-step technical procedures for a specific task, whereas a playbook outlines the overall response to a type of incident. A policy states management intent. A risk register tracks risks. A business impact analysis assesses the effects of disruptions.

prompt: A plant wants its internal red team to emulate an attacker against its OT test bed while the SOC analysts watch in real time, with both teams discussing each technique to improve detections immediately. Which exercise type is this?

options.text: Vulnerability scan
Purple-team exercise
External audit
Tabletop exercise

explanation: A purple-team exercise has offensive and defensive teams work together, sharing each technique to tune detections and response in real time. A tabletop exercise is discussion-based and involves no live attack. An external audit reviews compliance. A vulnerability scan identifies weaknesses without emulating an attacker or improving detections collaboratively.

prompt: Plant managers, operators, engineers and communications staff gather in a conference room and walk through a ransomware scenario affecting the HMIs, discussing what each person would do as the facilitator injects new events. Which activity is this?

options.text: Tabletop exercise
Process validation
Purple-team exercise
Penetration test

explanation: A tabletop exercise is a facilitated, discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario that tests plans, roles and decisions without touching systems. A penetration test actively attacks systems. A purple-team exercise involves live technical activity. Process validation confirms a process runs correctly after a change.

prompt: A utility wants operators and responders to practice hands-on detection and recovery from a simulated attack, using a replica of its SCADA system connected to a process model, without any risk to the real grid. Which preparedness activity is this?

options.text: Risk register review
Simulation exercise
Business impact analysis
Tabletop exercise

explanation: A simulation exercise uses a replica environment or process model so participants can practice technical actions realistically without affecting production. A tabletop exercise is discussion-based. A risk register review examines documented risks. A business impact analysis assesses the effects of disruptions.

prompt: An OT security manager has limited time to prepare detailed playbooks. Which approach best focuses preparation?

options.text: Prioritize high-value assets and the most exposed attack surface
Write playbooks only for printers and office PCs first
Write one generic playbook covering all corporate IT systems
Delay all playbooks until after the next real incident occurs

explanation: Preparation should start with the high-value assets whose compromise would cause the greatest harm and the parts of the attack surface most likely to be used. Printers and office PCs are lower priority. A generic IT playbook ignores OT needs. Waiting for an incident leaves the plant unprepared.

prompt: An OT incident response team is assembling its flyaway kit for responding at plant sites. Which TWO items belong in the kit? (Choose two.)

options.text: A production PLC spare already loaded with the plant's current logic
Site-appropriate PPE such as a hard hat, safety glasses, flame-resistant clothing and hearing protection
Personal smartphones for photographing HMI screens to post online
Tooling such as a hardware write blocker, a network tap, serial cables and a laptop with offline vendor software
The only copy of the plant's backups

explanation: A flyaway kit holds what responders need to work safely and collect evidence on site: PPE suited to the plant and tooling such as write blockers, taps, cables and an offline laptop. Spare production PLCs belong in plant stores, not a generic kit. The only copy of backups should never travel in a field kit. Posting HMI photos online is inappropriate.

prompt: During an incident, the plant manager must decide quickly whether to keep a unit running in manual mode or shut it down. What best supports this decision?

options.text: Waiting until the forensic investigation is complete
The opinion of whichever manager arrives first
A predefined decision matrix with shutdown criteria
A vote among all employees on shift

explanation: A decision matrix agreed in advance defines the conditions, such as loss of view, loss of control or SIS status, that trigger a shutdown, allowing fast, consistent decisions. Relying on whoever arrives first is inconsistent. A vote is too slow and lacks authority. Waiting for forensics delays a safety-critical decision.

prompt: A US company whose OT systems are encrypted by ransomware is considering paying the demand. Which step must its decision process include before any payment?

options.text: Asking the attackers to confirm they are not sanctioned
Paying through a personal account to avoid company records
Paying immediately to minimize production downtime
Legal checks of whether recipients are OFAC-sanctioned

explanation: Paying a ransom to a sanctioned person or group can violate US sanctions administered by OFAC, so legal review, often with law enforcement and the insurer, is required before any payment. Paying immediately skips this review. Attackers' assurances are worthless. Using a personal account to hide the payment is improper and does not avoid legal liability.

prompt: A responder removes a suspect USB drive from an HMI, bags it and hands it to a forensic analyst. What must be recorded to preserve the evidence's integrity for possible legal use?

options.text: The drive's color, brand and capacity
Each transfer of custody, with time, people and purpose
Nothing further, because the drive is already labeled
Only the receiving analyst's name and team

explanation: A chain of custody record documents every transfer, including who handled the evidence, when and why, so its integrity can be demonstrated. A label alone does not show who handled the item. Recording only the analyst omits the collector and timing. Color and brand describe the drive but not its handling.

prompt: During an incident, the HMI continues to show normal tank levels and pump states, but field operators find a tank overflowing. Which primary impact does this represent?

options.text: Loss of safety
Denial of service against the historian
Loss of view
Manipulation of view

explanation: Manipulation of view means operators are shown false information while the real process differs, as here. Loss of view means operators cannot see the process at all, such as a blank or frozen HMI. Loss of safety means safety functions cannot act. A historian denial of service affects stored data, not the live display.

prompt: An attacker disables the safety instrumented system's trip functions so that it will not act on a high-pressure condition, although the basic control system keeps running normally. Which primary impact is this?

options.text: Loss of safety
Loss of view
Loss of control
Manipulation of view

explanation: Loss of safety means safety functions can no longer protect against hazardous conditions, as when SIS trips are disabled. Loss of view and manipulation of view concern what operators can see. Loss of control means operators cannot command the process, yet the basic control system still works here.

prompt: Responders suspect fileless malware is running on an engineering workstation that is still powered on. What should they collect first?

options.text: The workstation's warranty records
A photo of the workstation's keyboard
A memory image, before shutting it down
A disk image after rebooting the workstation

explanation: Volatile memory holds running processes, network connections and fileless malware, and it is lost on shutdown, so memory should be captured first. A keyboard photo has little evidentiary value. Warranty records are irrelevant. Rebooting before collection destroys the memory evidence.

prompt: Investigators need to reconstruct the exact order in which breakers opened and protection relays operated during a substation incident, down to the millisecond. Which process data set is most useful?

options.text: The plant's purchase orders for relays
Badge access records from the administration building
Corporate email server logs for the night
Sequence of events records correlated with historian data

explanation: Sequence of events records provide precise, time-stamped records of breaker and relay operations, and correlating them with historian data reconstructs the process timeline. Email logs do not record breaker operations. Administration building badge records show physical entries only. Purchase orders are unrelated.

prompt: The approved network design states that the PLC zone has no external connections. During an investigation, flow data shows a PLC exchanging traffic with an internet IP address. What does this represent?

options.text: A deviation from design indicating an unknown path
A firewall logging error at the boundary
Normal background traffic from the PLC
Expected vendor telemetry from the controller

explanation: Traffic that the approved design says cannot exist is a deviation from design and points to an undocumented path, such as a hidden modem or misconfigured rule. It cannot be normal background traffic because the design permits no external connections. Vendor telemetry would be documented and should not come directly from a PLC. Flow data records actual traffic, so a firewall logging error does not explain it.

prompt: An HMI has communicated with the same three PLCs for months. During an incident, flow records show it suddenly connecting to 40 hosts across several subnets. How should this be classified?

options.text: A deviation from the SIS safety requirements specification
Anomalous behavior that deviates from the baseline
Expected behavior after a Windows update
A sign that the HMI license has expired

explanation: A sharp change from an established communication pattern is anomalous behavior relative to the baseline, consistent with scanning or lateral movement. Windows updates do not make HMIs contact dozens of internal hosts. The SIS safety requirements specification is unrelated. An expired license would reduce, not expand, communications.

prompt: In a packet capture from a cell network, an analyst finds S7comm messages that place a Siemens CPU into STOP mode, sent from a workstation that is not the engineering workstation. Why is industrial protocol analysis important here?

options.text: It encrypts the captured traffic for storage
It proves that the CPU hardware is faulty
It reveals the exact commands sent and their source
It shows the type of network cable in use

explanation: Decoding industrial protocols reveals the actual commands, such as a CPU stop, and which host sent them, which generic flow data cannot show. Packet captures do not identify cable types. Analysis does not encrypt traffic. A stop command from an unauthorized host points to misuse, not faulty hardware.

prompt: A decoy PLC with no legitimate function has been deployed on the control network. During an incident, the decoy logs connection attempts and a program upload request from an HMI. Why is this data valuable?

options.text: It proves that the IDS sensors are misconfigured
It indicates normal operator activity on the network
It shows the decoy is working as a production controller
Any contact with a decoy is a high-confidence indicator

explanation: Deception technology produces high-fidelity alerts because legitimate systems have no reason to interact with a decoy. The decoy is not a production controller. Operators have no reason to connect to it. Decoy alerts are independent of IDS configuration.

prompt: A remote pump station connects to the internet through a small business router that keeps no logs. Investigators suspect data was sent to an external server during the incident. Where can they obtain records of the station's external traffic?

options.text: The HMI's alarm summary for the station
The ISP's logs, requested through proper legal channels
The plant's lockout/tagout records for the station
The pump station's VFD fault and trip log

explanation: When local devices keep no logs, the ISP may retain connection or flow records, which can be requested through legal or contractual channels. A VFD fault log records drive faults. The HMI alarm summary records process alarms. Lockout/tagout records document energy isolation, not network traffic.

prompt: A Linux-based data gateway in the IDMZ may have been compromised. The analyst wants to know which user ran commands with elevated privileges and what those commands were. Which log should be reviewed?

options.text: The PLC's scan time statistics
The web browser history on an operator HMI
Sudo entries in the authentication log
The switch's spanning tree change log

explanation: On Linux, sudo records the invoking user and command in the authentication log, typically /var/log/auth.log on Debian-based systems or /var/log/secure on Red Hat-based systems. HMI browser history is on a different system. PLC scan time statistics say nothing about Linux commands. Spanning tree logs record switch topology changes.

prompt: On a Linux historian, the analyst suspects the attacker created a service that starts automatically at boot. Which data source most directly shows when a new unit was started and what it ran?

options.text: The systemd journal (journalctl)
The PLC's I/O force table
The HMI alarm history export
The DNS reverse lookup zone

explanation: The systemd journal records unit and service start events and their output, so journalctl can reveal a newly created service. HMI alarm history records process alarms. A PLC's force table shows forced I/O values. A reverse lookup zone maps IP addresses to names.

prompt: Security logs on a Windows engineering workstation show that a new local user account was created and then added to the local Administrators group shortly before unusual logic changes. What should the analyst conclude?

options.text: The workstation's clock has drifted out of sync
An attacker may have created a privileged persistence account
The workstation's disk is failing
This is normal account maintenance that needs no review

explanation: Creating a new local account and adding it to Administrators just before unusual changes is a common persistence and privilege escalation pattern, recorded in Windows security events such as 4720 and 4732. Unapproved account creation should not be treated as normal. Clock drift changes timestamps but does not create accounts. Disk failure does not generate account management events.

prompt: Ransomware is spreading rapidly through a company's corporate network. The OT network is not yet affected but is connected to the corporate network through the industrial DMZ. What is the most appropriate immediate containment action?

options.text: Shut down every PLC in the plant
Wait for the ransomware to finish before acting
Open additional firewall rules so that OT can receive emergency patches from IT
Disconnect IT from OT at the IDMZ while operations continues

explanation: Severing the IT-to-OT conduit at the IDMZ keeps the ransomware from reaching OT while the plant continues to run locally, which is why plans should define how OT operates when disconnected. Shutting down every PLC causes unnecessary disruption. Waiting lets the ransomware spread. Opening more rules increases the paths for spread.

prompt: An infected engineering workstation must be kept running for forensic memory analysis, but it must not communicate with any production system. Which containment approach best meets both needs?

options.text: Quarantine it in a segment that allows only forensic access
Reset all operator passwords and leave the workstation in place
Reimage it immediately
Leave it connected and monitor it

explanation: Quarantine places the system in a controlled segment where analysts can examine it while it cannot reach production systems. Leaving it connected allows further spread or tampering. Reimaging immediately destroys volatile evidence. Resetting passwords does not stop the workstation from communicating.

prompt: Investigators confirm that an attacker is using a compromised vendor remote access account to reach the plant's jump host. Which TWO containment actions should be taken immediately? (Choose two.)

options.text: Suspend the compromised vendor account
Block the attacker's source addresses and the remote access path at the boundary firewall
Delete the jump host's logs
Shut down the entire plant
Email the vendor account's password to the vendor

explanation: Suspending the compromised account and blocking the attacker's traffic and access path stop the intrusion without disrupting the process. Shutting down the plant is excessive when containment is possible. Deleting logs destroys evidence. Emailing a password exposes it again.

prompt: Malware has been removed from all affected hosts. Investigators found that the attacker had harvested credentials, including domain administrator, service and shared HMI accounts. What should eradication include?

options.text: Resetting only the domain administrator password
Writing the new passwords on the HMI screens
Resetting every potentially compromised credential
Keeping all passwords to avoid disrupting services

explanation: Eradication must remove the attacker's access, which means resetting every potentially compromised credential, including service and shared accounts, with coordination to avoid breaking services. Resetting only the domain admin leaves other stolen credentials usable. Keeping passwords leaves the attacker's access in place. Writing passwords on screens discloses them.

prompt: Responders suspect that a PLC's firmware was modified by an attacker, and the vendor provides no tool to verify firmware integrity on that model. Which eradication approach is most reliable?

options.text: Download the same logic again over the existing firmware
Replace it with a known-good unit from trusted stock
Restart the PLC and assume the problem is resolved
Leave it in place and monitor for odd behavior

explanation: When firmware integrity cannot be verified, replacing the device with a known-good unit is the reliable way to remove the compromise. Restarting does not remove modified firmware. Reloading logic leaves the suspect firmware in place. Monitoring alone leaves a potentially malicious device in control.

prompt: An HMI server was compromised, and the team is unsure whether its recent backups contain the attacker's tools. Which recovery approach best ensures a clean system?

options.text: Bare metal rebuild from a verified golden image, then validated data
Leave the compromised server running and add an antivirus product
Copy the infected server's disk image onto new server hardware
Restore the most recent full backup without checking its contents

explanation: A bare metal rebuild from a trusted golden image, followed by restoring only validated data, avoids reintroducing the attacker's tools. Restoring an unchecked backup may restore the compromise. Adding antivirus to a compromised server does not guarantee removal. Copying the infected disk transfers the compromise.

prompt: A redundant controller pair runs a critical process. One controller must be replaced after it was found compromised, but the process cannot stop. Which recovery technique allows this?

options.text: Redesigning the entire control network first
Shutting down the whole process for a week
Hot swap it while the redundant partner keeps control
Bare metal restore of the historian server

explanation: Hot swapping replaces a component while the system keeps running, here with the redundant partner controlling the process. A historian restore does not replace the controller. A week-long shutdown is the outcome the plant needs to avoid. A network redesign may follow from lessons learned but does not replace the controller now.

prompt: Immediately after an incident is resolved, the response team holds a short meeting while details are fresh to capture what worked, what did not and urgent follow-ups. A detailed written review is planned for later. What is the short meeting called?

options.text: Postmortem
Root cause analysis report
Tabletop exercise
Hot wash

explanation: A hot wash is an immediate, informal debrief held right after an event, while a postmortem is a more detailed review conducted later. A root cause analysis report is a formal analysis document. A tabletop exercise is a discussion of a hypothetical scenario before incidents occur.

prompt: After a major OT incident at a natural gas utility, which TWO notifications are most likely to be mandatory? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reports to regulators or government agencies required by applicable rules
A notice to every employee's family members
A public post on the company's social media accounts
Notice to the cyber insurer within the time set in the policy
A phone call to competing utilities

explanation: Mandatory reporting typically includes regulatory or government reports required by law and notice to insurers as required by the policy, along with any contractual obligations. A social media post is a communications choice, not a mandatory report. Calling competitors is not required. Notifying employees' families is not a reporting obligation.

prompt: After heavy rain, a technician must reach an RTU in a below-grade valve vault. The vault floor is under several centimeters of water, and the RTU panel is still energized. What should the technician do?

options.text: Enter wearing rubber boots, since boots fully insulate against shock
Open the panel from the vault entrance and work on it from the ladder
Enter quickly and reset the RTU before the water rises further
Wait until power is isolated and the water is pumped out

explanation: Standing water near energized equipment creates a serious shock and drowning hazard, so power must be isolated and verified and the water removed, with confined space procedures followed. Rubber boots do not guarantee protection in standing water. Rushing in to reset the RTU ignores the hazard entirely. Working from the ladder still exposes the technician to the energized, flooded panel.

prompt: A contractor needs to weld a new support bracket in a cable tray area directly above the plant's main control panels. Which control is most appropriate before the work starts?

options.text: Disable the area's smoke detectors so welding fumes do not cause a trip
A hot work permit with combustibles protected and a fire watch posted
Increase the HMI alarm volume so operators hear any fire alarm
Ask operators to watch the CCTV feed of the cable tray area

explanation: Hot work near cables and control equipment needs a hot work permit, protection of combustibles and a dedicated fire watch. A louder HMI alarm does not prevent a fire. Disabling detectors without a permit-controlled impairment process removes protection. Operators watching CCTV are not a trained fire watch at the work location.

prompt: Before starting a network cutover in a running compressor building, the crew lead gathers everyone to review the job steps, hazards from the JSA, each person's role and everyone's authority to stop work. What is this meeting?

options.text: Pre-job briefing
Change advisory board review
Hot wash
Outbrief

explanation: A pre-job briefing is held before work begins to review steps, hazards, roles and stop-work authority. An outbrief happens at the end of the work to hand over status. A hot wash is an immediate debrief after an incident or exercise. A change advisory board approves changes but does not brief the crew on site hazards.

prompt: A municipal water utility wants to coordinate its cybersecurity efforts with the US federal agency designated as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Water and Wastewater Systems sector. Which agency is this?

options.text: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
Department of Energy
Environmental Protection Agency
Transportation Security Administration

explanation: The Environmental Protection Agency is the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Water and Wastewater Systems sector. The Department of Energy leads the Energy sector. The Transportation Security Administration oversees pipeline and transportation security. FERC regulates interstate electricity and approves NERC reliability standards.

prompt: In a flow control loop, which field device converts the controller's output signal into physical action on the process?

options.text: The operator workstation that displays the loop faceplate
The flow transmitter that measures the flow rate
The control valve and its positioner
The historian that records the flow trend

explanation: An actuator, such as a control valve with its positioner, turns the controller's output into physical movement. The flow transmitter is a sensor that measures the process. A historian stores data. An operator workstation displays information and sends supervisory commands but does not act on the process directly.

prompt: A packaging machine has its own PLC, servo drives, safety relay and a panel HMI connected by a small Ethernet switch inside the machine cabinet. The switch has no connection to the plant network. How is this best described?

options.text: A localized control network
A distributed control system
A manufacturing execution system
A supervisory control and data acquisition system

explanation: A small network that serves one machine or cell and does not connect to the wider plant is a localized control network. SCADA supervises geographically dispersed assets. A DCS integrates many controllers across a site for process control. An MES manages production orders and tracking.

prompt: An attacker steals the HMI project's tag database, which maps names such as FEED_PUMP_101_RUN and REACTOR_TEMP_PV to controller addresses. Why is this a significant loss?

options.text: Losing the tag database immediately stops all PLCs from running
It shows what each address does, aiding targeted manipulation
Tag databases contain the plant's payroll and personnel records
Tag databases store the HMI's operating system license keys

explanation: Tags give meaningful names to controller memory and I/O addresses, so the database tells an attacker which address starts a pump or reports a temperature. Tag databases do not hold payroll records. Copying the database does not stop the PLCs. License keys are not what makes tags sensitive.

prompt: During an investigation, an engineer connects to a PLC with its programming software and reads the live value of the reactor temperature tag, then compares it with the value the HMI is displaying. What is the engineer checking?

options.text: The tag's archived historian average
The tag's set point limits
The tag's configured alarm deadband
The tag's current value in the controller

explanation: Reading the live value in the controller shows the tag's current value, which can expose an HMI that is displaying falsified data. An alarm deadband is a configuration parameter. A historian average is a stored aggregate rather than the live value. Set point limits constrain operator entries and are not measurements.

prompt: A controls engineer builds a boiler control strategy by placing PID, scaling and selector blocks on a canvas and wiring their inputs and outputs together graphically. Which IEC 61131-3 language is this?

options.text: Structured text
Function block diagram
Instruction list
Ladder diagram

explanation: Function block diagram represents logic as graphical blocks connected by signal lines, which suits continuous control such as PID strategies. Structured text is textual. Ladder diagram uses rungs of contacts and coils. Instruction list is a low-level textual language.

prompt: A plant still runs older Allen-Bradley controllers on Data Highway Plus. Engineers reach them from the Ethernet network through a bridge module. Which statement best describes the security situation?

options.text: DH+ is legacy and unauthenticated, so the bridge must be restricted
DH+ uses TCP port 502, so a Modbus firewall rule protects it
DH+ cannot be reached from Ethernet under any circumstances
DH+ is natively encrypted, so the bridge needs no protection

explanation: Data Highway Plus is a legacy Rockwell token-passing peer network with no built-in authentication, so the bridge that connects it to Ethernet becomes its access point and must be restricted. DH+ is not encrypted. It does not use TCP 502, which is Modbus TCP. Bridge modules exist precisely to reach DH+ from Ethernet.

prompt: A machine builder uses an Ethernet-based fieldbus in which each slave device reads and inserts its data as a single frame passes through it, enabling cycle times well under a millisecond for motion control. Which protocol is this?

options.text: OPC Unified Architecture
BACnet/IP
EtherCAT
Modbus TCP

explanation: EtherCAT processes frames on the fly as they pass through each slave, giving very short, deterministic cycle times for motion control. BACnet/IP is for building automation. OPC UA is an integration and information-modeling protocol, not a sub-millisecond fieldbus. Modbus TCP uses ordinary request-response transactions.

prompt: A port authority's traffic system shows a ship apparently sailing across a runway, based on AIS broadcasts received over VHF. Which weakness allows this kind of false position report?

options.text: AIS position data comes from the port's own radar
AIS uses strong encryption that has been broken
